questions.title: Shot noise and the 1/√N scaling law
questions.prompt: You run the same Bell-state circuit on Qiskit's Aer simulator twice: once with 100 shots, once with 8192 shots. Both times the true probability of each outcome is 0.5. Explain, using the standard error formula sqrt(p(1-p)/N), why the two runs give visibly different counts distributions even with no noise model attached, and why doubling your shot count from 1024 to 2048 would NOT cut your statistical uncertainty in half.
questions.modelAnswer: A 'shot' is one full, independent execution of the circuit from initialization through measurement, and the counts dictionary you get back is just a tally of which bitstring came out on each shot. Even with zero hardware noise, the measured frequency of an outcome is a random variable, and its expected spread around the true probability p is given by the standard error SE = sqrt(p(1-p)/N). At N=100 with p=0.5, SE ≈ 0.05 (about ±9.8 percentage points for a 95% interval); at N=8192, SE ≈ 0.0055 (about ±1.1 points). That's why a 100-shot run might show something like 47/53 while an 8192-shot run lands much closer to 50/50 — the spread shrinks as shots increase, but only as 1/sqrt(N), not linearly. Going from 100 to 1024 shots (≈10x) only cuts SE by about sqrt(10)≈3.2x. So doubling 1024 to 2048 shots only multiplies N by 2, which shrinks SE by sqrt(2)≈1.41x, not 2x — to actually halve the standard error you need 4x the shots, i.e. roughly 4096, not 2048.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through the math out loud because it trips people up constantly. Every shot is an independent coin-flip-like trial, so the counts you see follow binomial statistics, and the standard error of the observed frequency is sqrt(p(1-p)/N). At 100 shots that error is around 5 percentage points, which is why a 50/50 circuit can easily show 47/53 on one run. At 8192 shots it's closer to half a point, so you'd expect something much closer to 4096/4096. The part that catches people off guard is the scaling: because SE depends on sqrt(N), not N, you get diminishing returns fast —  10x the shots only buys you about 3.2x the precision, and to literally halve your uncertainty you need 4x the shots, not 2x. I bring this up early with teams because shots aren't free — on real hardware they cost queue time and credits — so I want people choosing a shot count based on the precision their application actually needs, not an arbitrary round number like 1024 just because it's a default.
questions.example: At N=100 one real seeded draw from a true 50/50 distribution gave {'0': 47, '1': 53}; at N=8192 a draw gave {'0': 4026, '1': 4166} (≈50.85%), consistent with the much narrower ±1.1-point band at that shot count.
commonMistakes: Assuming more shots always gets 'closer to the right number' linearly
Thinking doubling shots halves the uncertainty (it only reduces it by a factor of sqrt(2))
Treating any single run's observed frequency as the 'true' probability rather than a noisy estimate
Ignoring that shots cost real queue time/money on hardware, so over-shooting has a real cost
keyPoints: A shot is one independent full circuit execution ending in measurement
Standard error of an observed frequency is sqrt(p(1-p)/N)
Error shrinks with sqrt(N), so 4x shots are needed to halve uncertainty, not 2x
Shot count is a real engineering tradeoff against time/cost, not a free precision dial

evaluationCriteria.criterion: States the correct standard error formula
Explains why 100 vs 8192 shots look visibly different with no noise model
Correctly computes that halving SE requires 4x the shots, not 2x
Connects this to the real cost of shots on hardware

questions.title: Why a Toffoli gate is not 'one gate' on real hardware
questions.prompt: A colleague says their circuit is 'small' because it only has 4 Toffoli (CCX) gates written in their QuantumCircuit. Using the standard Toffoli decomposition, explain why this circuit could still produce a surprisingly large number of CNOT gates once transpiled, and why the final answer also depends on which backend they target.
questions.modelAnswer: A single Toffoli gate is not a native hardware gate on superconducting backends — it's standardly decomposed into 6 CNOT gates plus several single-qubit H, T, and T† gates once transpiled into a basis gate set of CX plus single-qubit gates. So 4 Toffolis in the source circuit become at least 4×6 = 24 CNOTs (plus the single-qubit gates) after transpilation, before accounting for any additional SWAP gates the router has to insert if those Toffoli's target qubits aren't adjacent on the backend's coupling map. 'How many gates does my circuit have' only has a meaningful answer after calling transpile() and checking compiled.count_ops() for a specific backend and optimization_level — two different backends can transpile the exact same circuit into different gate counts and depths because they have different native basis gates and different connectivity.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back gently on 'small' right away. In the QuantumCircuit object, sure, it's 4 gates — but that circuit is an abstract plan, not what actually runs. A Toffoli isn't native to superconducting hardware, so the transpiler rewrites each one into roughly 6 CNOTs plus some single-qubit H/T/T† gates — that's a well-documented textbook identity, not a guess. Four Toffolis alone is already 24+ CNOTs before routing even enters the picture. If those Toffoli's qubits aren't physically adjacent on the target backend, the transpiler also has to insert SWAP gates to route them together, and each SWAP is itself built from more CNOTs. So the honest answer to 'how big is this circuit' is: run transpile(qc, backend=backend, optimization_level=3) and look at compiled.count_ops() and compiled.depth() for the actual backend you're targeting — not the circuit you wrote. I've seen people size up a circuit from source code and be off by 5-10x once it's actually compiled for hardware.
questions.example: qc.ccx(0,1,2) written once in source becomes, after transpile(qc, backend=backend, optimization_level=3), several CX plus single-qubit gates when you print compiled.count_ops() — the exact count depends on the backend's basis gates and coupling map.
commonMistakes: Equating source-circuit gate count with what actually runs on hardware
Forgetting the Toffoli decomposes to 6 CNOTs, not 1-to-1 with a native gate
Not accounting for additional SWAP overhead from routing on top of basis-gate rewriting
Assuming gate count is backend-independent
keyPoints: A CCX gate decomposes into 6 CNOTs plus single-qubit H/T/T† gates
Multiple Toffolis compound this cost quickly
Routing/SWAP insertion is a second, separate source of gate-count growth
Gate count is only meaningful post-transpilation, for a specific backend and optimization_level

evaluationCriteria.criterion: States the correct Toffoli-to-CNOT decomposition fact
Computes the compounding effect across 4 Toffolis
Mentions routing/SWAP as a second compounding factor
Explains gate count is backend- and optimization_level-dependent

questions.title: Statevector vs. QASM (shot-based) simulation
questions.prompt: A teammate wants to know the exact amplitudes of every basis state in a 4-qubit circuit's final state, and separately wants to know what a real device's measurement histogram would plausibly look like at 4096 shots. Explain which Qiskit Aer simulation mode answers each question and why you can't get exact amplitudes from a shots-based run no matter how many shots you use.
questions.modelAnswer: The statevector simulator directly computes and returns the full complex amplitude vector of the quantum state — it tracks the exact mathematical state through every gate and gives you every amplitude with no sampling involved, which is exactly what answers 'what are the exact amplitudes.' A QASM-style (shots-based) simulation instead repeatedly samples the circuit's implied probability distribution N times and returns a counts dictionary of observed bitstrings, mimicking what a real measurement-only device would give you. No matter how large N gets, a shots-based run only ever approaches the true probabilities asymptotically via the 1/sqrt(N) standard-error scaling — it never returns the underlying complex amplitudes themselves, because measurement collapses the state and only classical bitstring outcomes are observable. So for amplitude-level questions you need the statevector simulator; for 'what would a real device's histogram look like' you need a shots-based run at a specified shot count.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd split this into two separate requests because they genuinely need two different tools. If you want to see the actual amplitudes — the exact complex numbers Qiskit is tracking at every qubit's basis state — you run the statevector simulator, which isn't sampling anything, it's just reporting the linear-algebra result directly. That's what you want for debugging circuit logic, because a wrong amplitude there is unambiguously a bug in your circuit, not noise. If instead you want to know what a real device's histogram would plausibly look like, you need a shots-based simulation at a specific shot count, because a real device can only ever report classical measurement outcomes, never amplitudes — running more shots narrows the statistical gap to the true probabilities, but it will never hand you amplitudes, because the amplitudes aren't directly observable quantities in the first place; only probabilities (via repeated measurement) are.
commonMistakes: Assuming more shots eventually reveals exact amplitudes
Not realizing amplitudes include phase information that counts/histograms can never show
Using statevector simulation to model what real noisy hardware output looks like
Confusing probability (observable via shots) with amplitude (only accessible via statevector simulation)
keyPoints: Statevector simulation returns exact amplitudes via direct computation, no sampling
Shots-based (QASM-style) simulation samples a counts dictionary, mimicking real measurement
Shots-based results only approach true probabilities asymptotically, never amplitudes
Choice of simulator depends on whether you need amplitude-level debugging or realistic measurement statistics

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly matches each question to the right simulation mode
Explains statevector sim computes exact amplitudes with no sampling

questions.title: Hand-build a 2-qubit Grover circuit
questions.prompt: Write a complete Qiskit circuit that performs one Grover iteration on a 2-qubit, 4-item search space (|00>, |01>, |10>, |11>) to find the marked item |11>, then explain why this specific case gives an exact, deterministic result.
questions.code:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit

qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
qc.h([0, 1])          # uniform superposition over 4 states
qc.cz(0, 1)           # oracle: phase-flips the marked state |11>
qc.h([0, 1]); qc.x([0, 1]); qc.cz(0, 1); qc.x([0, 1]); qc.h([0, 1])   # diffuser
qc.measure([0, 1], [0, 1])
questions.modelAnswer: The circuit starts with H on both qubits to create an equal superposition across all 4 states, each at probability 0.25. The oracle, a single controlled-Z (qc.cz(0,1)), phase-flips only the |11> amplitude's sign without changing any probabilities yet — all four outcomes are still equally likely to measure right after the oracle. The five-gate diffuser block (H, X, CZ, X, H on both qubits) performs 'inversion about the mean,' reflecting every amplitude around the average amplitude, which converts that single phase flip into a large boost in the marked state's measurement probability. For N=4 items with exactly 1 marked item, the optimal iteration count formula (π/4)·√(N/M) evaluates to exactly 1, and running this exact circuit gives probability 1.0 on |11> and 0 on every other outcome — a genuinely exact result, not an approximation, confirmed by direct matrix simulation. This is a special case; for larger N the optimal iteration count is a real number rounded to a nearby integer, so the result lands close to but not exactly at probability 1.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this piece by piece and narrate what each block is doing, because that's what shows real understanding rather than memorized syntax. First, qc.h([0,1]) puts the system into uniform superposition — no outcome favored. Then qc.cz(0,1) is the oracle: a controlled-Z only flips the sign of the |11> amplitude, and crucially it doesn't collapse anything or reveal which state is marked — if you measured right after the oracle you'd still see 25% on each outcome. The real engine is the diffuser, that five-gate block starting with another H — it reflects every amplitude around their average, so the one negative-signed amplitude from the oracle gets amplified into a measurable probability boost on |11>. For this specific tiny case, N=4 with 1 marked item, the math works out so that exactly one iteration gives probability 1.0 — I'd flag that this is a clean textbook special case, and that for bigger search spaces I'd reach for qiskit_algorithms.Grover and AmplificationProblem rather than hand-deriving the oracle and diffuser, because deriving a custom diffuser for a real problem doesn't scale by hand.
questions.example: Running this circuit on Qiskit's Aer simulator returns the bitstring '11' on every single shot, with zero statistical spread, confirming the exact probability-1.0 result for this N=4, M=1 case.
commonMistakes: Measuring right after the oracle and expecting to see the marked state favored (it isn't — only the phase changed)
Forgetting the diffuser is also needed — the oracle alone does nothing measurable
Assuming this exact probability-1.0 result generalizes to every N and M
Hand-building the oracle/diffuser for large N instead of using qiskit_algorithms.Grover
keyPoints: H gates create the initial uniform superposition
The oracle (CZ) phase-flips the marked state without revealing it
The diffuser performs inversion-about-the-mean to convert phase into probability
N=4, M=1 with 1 iteration is an exact special case (probability exactly 1.0)

questions.title: Applying QFT to a basis state with Qiskit
questions.prompt: Write the Qiskit code to apply a 3-qubit QFT to the basis state representing decimal 1, and describe what the resulting state's amplitudes and phases look like. Why does this NOT mean the QFT destroyed the information about the input?
questions.code:
from qiskit.circuit.library import QFT
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit

qc = QuantumCircuit(3)
qc.x(0)                       # prepare |001> (decimal 1)
qc.append(QFT(num_qubits=3), [0, 1, 2])
questions.modelAnswer: qiskit.circuit.library.QFT(num_qubits=3) is the ready-to-use circuit for the transform — you don't need to hand-build the controlled-phase-gate ladder yourself. Starting from the basis state |001> (decimal 1, probability 1.0 on that state, 0 elsewhere) and applying the 3-qubit QFT gives a verified exact result: every one of the 8 basis states now has the same amplitude magnitude, 0.353553 (1/√8), so every outcome has the same measurement probability, 0.125. If you only look at probabilities it looks like the input was erased into uniform randomness. But the 8 terms have different phases — the |000> term comes out purely real (0.353553 + 0i) while the other 7 terms trace out a phase ramp of the form e^(2πi·k·x/N) where x=1 is the input and k indexes the output state. That phase ramp, not the magnitude, is where the information about the input value actually lives — the QFT re-encodes 'which outcome is certain' into 'what phase relationship exists across all outcomes,' which is only useful because algorithms like phase estimation are specifically built to extract that phase relationship back out.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write it exactly the way the library intends — prepare |001> with an X gate on qubit 0, then append QFT(num_qubits=3) rather than hand-deriving the controlled-phase ladder, since core Qiskit already provides it. The result is the part people get wrong: every one of the 8 probabilities comes out to exactly 0.125, which looks identical to a maximally mixed random state if you only check probabilities. I'd point out that's deliberately misleading if you stop there — the real signature of the QFT is in the phases, not the magnitudes. The |000> term is purely real, and the other seven have a specific phase ramp, e^(2πi·k·x/N), that depends on the input value x=1. That phase structure is exactly the Fourier relationship, and it's recoverable — it's not noise, and it's not the same as what you'd get from just applying Hadamards to flatten the state, which would destroy that specific phase relationship. This distinction matters practically because phase estimation and Shor's algorithm are built specifically to extract that phase ramp back out.
commonMistakes: Concluding the QFT 'destroyed' the input because all probabilities came out equal
Not distinguishing amplitude magnitude from phase as two separate pieces of information
Treating QFT output as equivalent to applying Hadamards to every qubit
Forgetting QFT is available directly from qiskit.circuit.library, not qiskit_algorithms
keyPoints: QFT(num_qubits=n) is a core qiskit.circuit.library class, not part of qiskit-algorithms
Applying QFT to a basis state produces uniform magnitude (0.125 probability each) but non-uniform phase
The phase ramp e^(2πi·k·x/N) encodes the input value x
This differs fundamentally from applying Hadamards, which has simpler phase relationships

Correctly states the resulting uniform-magnitude/0.125-probability result

questions.title: Hand-computing a zero-noise extrapolation
questions.prompt: You gate-fold a circuit to measure an expectation value at three noise-scale factors: λ=1 gives E=0.72, λ=2 gives E=0.64, and λ=3 gives E=0.56. Using linear zero-noise extrapolation, compute the estimated zero-noise expectation value from the λ=1 and λ=2 points, and show that using λ=1 and λ=3 instead gives the same answer.
questions.code:
# Linear extrapolation: E(0) = 2*E(1) - E(2)
E1, E2, E3 = 0.72, 0.64, 0.56
estimate_12 = 2*E1 - E2
estimate_13 = E1 - (E3 - E1) / (3 - 1) * (1 - 0)  # equivalent linear fit through (1,E1),(3,E3)
print(estimate_12, estimate_13)
questions.modelAnswer: Using λ=1 and λ=2: E(0) = 2·E(1) − E(2) = 2(0.72) − 0.64 = 1.44 − 0.64 = 0.80. Using λ=1 and λ=3 instead: the line through (1, 0.72) and (3, 0.56) has slope (0.56−0.72)/(3−1) = −0.08, so E(0) = 0.72 − (−0.08)(1−0) = 0.72 + 0.08 = 0.80. Both pairs of points recover the same zero-noise estimate, 0.80, because this teaching example was deliberately constructed so E(λ) scales exactly linearly: E(λ) = 0.80 − 0.08·λ. In practice, gate folding (replacing gate G with G·G⁻¹·G, which triples effective noise at λ=3 while leaving the ideal computation unchanged) is how you actually generate the amplified-noise data points, and real hardware noise scaling is usually only approximately linear, so production tools like mitiq often use a Richardson extrapolation or exponential fit chosen based on the data's actual shape, rather than assuming linearity blindly.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd do the arithmetic directly: the two-point linear extrapolation formula is E(0) = 2·E(1) − E(2), so plugging in gives 2(0.72) − 0.64 = 0.80. Then I'd check the other pair just to make the point that it's not a coincidence of which points you pick — fitting a line through (1, 0.72) and (3, 0.56) gives the same slope, −0.08 per unit λ, and extrapolating back to λ=0 again gives 0.80. I'd be upfront that this example was built to be exactly linear on purpose, specifically so the hand arithmetic recovers the true value with zero residual error — real hardware isn't usually this clean, and at larger λ the decay often looks closer to exponential, which is why I'd reach for mitiq's built-in extrapolation fits, or qiskit-ibm-runtime's EstimatorV2 resilience_level option, rather than hand-rolling a linear fit against real noisy data.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the extrapolation formula E(0) = 2E(1) - E(2) and instead just averaging the points
Not recognizing that this specific example is deliberately linear, unlike most real hardware
Confusing gate folding (which amplifies noise) with error correction (which would remove it)
Assuming any two λ points will always agree this cleanly on real (non-linear) data
keyPoints: Linear ZNE formula: E(0) = 2·E(1) − E(2) for λ=1,2
Both verified point pairs (λ=1,2 and λ=1,3) recover the same 0.80 estimate
Gate folding (G·G⁻¹·G) is the mechanism used to amplify noise without changing the ideal computation
Real hardware noise scaling is often non-linear, requiring Richardson or exponential fits in production tools like mitiq

Correctly shows the λ=1,3 points give the same answer

questions.title: Readout-mitigated results look noisier than the raw counts
questions.prompt: You apply readout error mitigation (corrected = M⁻¹ · observed) to a 4096-shot measurement and notice the corrected probabilities actually have MORE spread around the true value than the raw observed counts did. Your teammate says this proves the mitigation code is broken. Walk through why this can happen even with correct mitigation code, and what it does and doesn't tell you about the fix.
questions.modelAnswer: This is not necessarily a bug. Readout mitigation corrects systematic bias — the known, fixed distortion introduced by the calibration/confusion matrix M — by applying M⁻¹ to whatever you observe. But it does not and cannot eliminate shot noise, the statistical sampling variation from only having a finite number of measurements. Worse, because matrix inversion can amplify small input variations, the correction step can make the random statistical-noise component of your estimate slightly larger than it was in the raw observed data, even while it correctly removes the systematic bias. For example, applying M⁻¹ to exact probabilities recovers the true distribution exactly, but applying the same M⁻¹ to sampled fractions from 4096 shots only gets close, not exact, and the correction can slightly inflate that residual noise. So the right diagnostic isn't 'is the corrected number noisier than raw' — it's whether the calibration matrix M itself is accurate and recent, and whether you're interpreting the correction as removing systematic bias only, not as a noise-free answer.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk the teammate through the distinction between two different kinds of error before assuming the code is wrong. Readout mitigation is designed to undo one specific thing: the systematic, known distortion captured in the calibration matrix M, by multiplying the observed distribution by M⁻¹. It was never designed to remove shot noise — the randomness that comes purely from having a finite number of shots — and because inverting a matrix can amplify small input variations, it's completely expected that the corrected numbers can show slightly more statistical spread than the raw counts did, even when M is exactly right. I'd verify the mitigation logic is correct by checking it against an exact-probability case first, where M⁻¹ · (exact observed) should recover the exact truth with no error at all. If that checks out, the 'noisier-looking' result at finite shots isn't a bug — it's an honest tradeoff: mitigation improves your estimate of the true value on average, it doesn't produce a noise-free one.
commonMistakes: Assuming mitigation should eliminate all noise, including shot noise
Concluding the code is broken just because corrected numbers show more spread than raw
Not testing the mitigation logic against exact (non-sampled) probabilities first to isolate the systematic-vs-statistical distinction
Not checking whether the calibration matrix M itself is stale or inaccurate
keyPoints: corrected = M⁻¹ · observed corrects systematic bias, not statistical shot noise
Matrix inversion can amplify small input variations, slightly increasing apparent noise
Verify mitigation logic against exact probabilities first, where it recovers the truth exactly
Mitigation improves the estimate on average; it does not produce a noise-free result

questions.title: Circuit depth exploded after transpiling for a new backend
questions.prompt: A circuit that compiled to a reasonable depth on Backend A balloons in gate count and depth when you transpile the same QuantumCircuit for Backend B, using the same optimization_level=3. Both backends are superconducting devices from the same provider. What are the two most likely causes, and how would you confirm which one is responsible?
questions.modelAnswer: The two most likely causes are a mismatched basis gate set and a worse coupling map (connectivity graph) on Backend B. Transpilation does two things at once: it rewrites every gate into the target backend's native basis gates, and it maps logical qubits onto physical qubits respecting that backend's coupling map. If Backend B's basis gates require a less efficient decomposition of some gates in your circuit, gate count alone can grow. Separately and often more significantly, if Backend B's coupling map is sparser or your chosen logical qubits don't map well onto adjacent physical qubits, the router has to insert more SWAP gates (each built from multiple native two-qubit gates) to physically relocate states for every two-qubit gate your circuit needs — this is one of the two reasons a transpiled circuit is almost always bigger than the circuit you wrote. To confirm which is responsible, inspect compiled.count_ops() for both backends to see if the native gate mix differs sharply (pointing to basis-gate rewriting), and separately check each backend's coupling map and compare compiled.depth() with and without routing enabled, or compare how many SWAP-derived gates appear — a circuit requiring many non-adjacent two-qubit interactions on a sparsely connected backend will show a sharp jump in gate count that's attributable specifically to routing, not basis-gate translation.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't guess — I'd go look at compiled.count_ops() for both backends side by side first. If the basis gates genuinely differ between Backend A and B, I'd expect a different mix of single-qubit gate types showing up, which tells me basis-gate rewriting is at least part of the story. But in my experience the bigger and more common culprit is connectivity: if Backend B's coupling map doesn't have the same adjacency pattern as A for the qubits my circuit wants to use, the transpiler has to insert a lot more SWAP gates to route two-qubit interactions onto physically adjacent qubits, and each SWAP is itself several CNOTs. I'd check both backends' coupling maps directly and see if my circuit's two-qubit gate pattern happens to line up with A's native connectivity more than B's. The real fix, once I know which one it is, might be choosing different physical qubits on B explicitly, rather than assuming 'same optimization_level' guarantees similar output across backends — it doesn't, because optimization_level controls how hard the transpiler works, not what hardware constraints it's working against.
commonMistakes: Assuming the same optimization_level produces comparable results across different backends
Not checking coupling maps as a likely source of the gap
Blaming the optimization_level setting itself rather than backend hardware differences
Not using compiled.count_ops()/compiled.depth() to actually diagnose instead of guessing
keyPoints: Transpilation rewrites gates to the backend's basis set AND maps qubits via the coupling map
A sparser or mismatched coupling map drives up SWAP-based routing overhead
Basis gate set differences can also independently inflate gate count
Diagnose with compiled.count_ops()/compiled.depth() and by comparing coupling maps directly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies basis gate set mismatch as one possible cause
Identifies coupling map/connectivity difference as the other likely cause
Proposes a concrete diagnostic using count_ops()/depth() or coupling map inspection

questions.title: Simulator result doesn't match hardware, and the team jumps straight to 'noise'
questions.prompt: Your team's circuit gives P(marked)≈95% on the Aer statevector simulator but a much lower, oddly-shaped distribution on real IBM hardware. Before accepting 'hardware noise' as the explanation, what two or three checks would you make first, and why might jumping straight to 'it's just noise' hide a real bug?
questions.modelAnswer: First, confirm the circuit submitted to hardware is the transpiled circuit (compiled, from transpile(qc, backend=backend)), not the original qc — a common mistake is accidentally submitting the untranspiled circuit, which can silently fail or behave unexpectedly on real hardware since it hasn't been mapped to native gates/physical qubits at all. Second, check the shot count and apply the same 1/sqrt(N) statistical-error reasoning used on the simulator — part of an 'oddly shaped' distribution might just be ordinary shot noise at a shot count too low for the precision you expect, not a hardware defect. Third, pull the backend's calibration report for the specific physical qubits your circuit landed on after transpilation — if those qubits or the edges between them have notably worse T1/T2 or two-qubit gate error than the device's median, that's a real, verifiable hardware cause rather than a vague 'noise' explanation. The reason to do all this before blaming noise: simulator-vs-hardware gaps are also commonly caused by a logic bug that the simulator doesn't catch because it's running your unoptimized circuit under ideal conditions, or by a measurement/bit-ordering mismatch between simulator output and real backend output. Attributing everything to noise without checking these risks missing an actual, fixable bug.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I'd accept 'it's just hardware noise,' I'd run through a short checklist. First: am I even running the same logical circuit on both? I'd confirm the hardware submission used the properly transpiled circuit for that specific backend, not the raw one — that's happened to people on my team before. Second, I'd sanity-check the shot count: is the 'odd shape' actually within the expected 1/sqrt(N) statistical band for the shots I used, or is it a real systematic skew? Third, I'd pull the calibration report for the exact physical qubits and edges my circuit got mapped onto and see if any of them are meaningfully worse than the device's median — that turns 'hardware noise' from a vague excuse into a specific, checkable cause. I push on this because 'noise' is a convenient catch-all, and I've seen real bugs — bit-ordering mismatches between how Qiskit reports measurement results and how a team expects them, or an accidentally untranspiled submission — get waved away as noise when they were actually fixable logic errors.

Overlooking bit-ordering or measurement-mapping mismatches as a non-noise explanation

questions.title: Choosing an optimization_level for a production submission pipeline
questions.prompt: You're designing a pipeline that submits many circuit variants to real IBM hardware every day. Compile time and queue cost both matter. How would you decide between optimization_level 0, 1, 2, and 3 across different stages of this pipeline, and why isn't 'always use level 3' automatically correct?
questions.modelAnswer: optimization_level controls how hard the transpiler works to shrink the resulting circuit: level 0 is minimal effort and fast to compile but produces larger, deeper circuits; level 3 does the most aggressive gate-count/depth reduction but is the slowest to compile. For real hardware, where every extra gate is another chance for error, higher levels usually matter more because a shorter, shallower circuit tends to produce cleaner results on noisy devices — so for anything actually submitted to real hardware, level 3 is usually the right default. But 'always use level 3' isn't automatically correct for every stage: during rapid local development and debugging, where you're iterating on circuit logic many times a minute and don't care about final gate count yet, a lower level (0 or 1) compiles much faster and lets you iterate quickly without hardware-grade optimization you don't need yet. A sound pipeline design uses a fast, low optimization_level for the dev/debug loop against a simulator, and reserves level 3 compilation specifically for the final submission step to real hardware, where the extra compile time is worth it because it directly reduces error accumulation and queue-time cost from needing to resubmit.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't hardcode one optimization_level across the whole pipeline. I'd split it by stage: while a circuit variant is still being developed or debugged against the Aer simulator, I'd use level 0 or 1 — compile speed matters more there than final gate count, since we're not paying hardware queue costs or accumulating real gate error yet. Once a circuit variant is validated and is about to go to real hardware, I'd switch to level 3 specifically for that submission, because on noisy hardware every extra gate and extra circuit depth is a real chance for error to accumulate, and the extra compile time is a small, one-time cost compared to the cost of a noisier result or a wasted queue slot. I'd push back on 'just always use level 3 everywhere' because it needlessly slows down the dev loop where the tradeoff doesn't pay for itself yet — the decision should track which stage of the pipeline you're actually in, not be a single global default.
commonMistakes: Using the same optimization_level for local dev iteration and real hardware submission
Assuming level 3 is strictly 'better' everywhere without weighing compile-time cost
Not recognizing that lower levels are a reasonable choice during fast iteration
Ignoring that queue cost on hardware makes the tradeoff asymmetric vs. simulator runs
keyPoints: optimization_level 0-3 trades compile speed against resulting gate count/depth
Higher levels matter more on real hardware where extra gates mean more accumulated error
Lower levels are appropriate during fast simulator-based dev iteration
A good pipeline varies optimization_level by stage rather than using one global setting

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what optimization_level trades off
Recommends level 3 specifically for real-hardware submission
Recommends a lower level for fast dev/debug iteration
Explains why a single global level isn't optimal for this pipeline

questions.title: Designing a dev-to-hardware pipeline stage progression
questions.prompt: Design the stages of a submission pipeline that takes a new circuit from 'just written' to 'running on real IBM hardware,' explaining what each stage is responsible for catching and why skipping a stage is a common, costly mistake.
questions.modelAnswer: A sound progression has at least three stages. Stage 1: statevector simulation on Aer, to verify the circuit's logic is exactly correct — since this is an exact computation with no noise, any wrong result here is unambiguously a bug in the circuit, not noise, so this is where logic errors must be caught. Stage 2: shots-based (QASM-style) simulation at a realistic shot count, to validate that the expected measurement statistics look right and to pick an appropriate shot count using the 1/sqrt(N) standard-error reasoning, still in a noise-free environment. Stage 3: transpile for the specific target backend at optimization_level=3 and inspect compiled.count_ops()/compiled.depth(), checking the mapped physical qubits against that backend's calibration report (T1/T2, readout error, edge error rates) before submitting. Only after all three stages pass does the job go to the real-hardware queue. Skipping straight to hardware from stage 1 is a common, costly mistake because queue times mean you wait for a job that might fail for a reason a free simulator run would have caught in seconds, and because noisy real-hardware output makes a logic bug and a hardware error look identical — you lose the ability to tell which one you're looking at.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd design this as three gates, not one big leap. First gate: does it even compute the right answer, checked on the exact statevector simulator — no noise, so any wrong result here is purely a logic bug I need to fix before going further. Second gate: does it look right under realistic measurement statistics, run as a shots-based simulation at the shot count I actually plan to use, so I can sanity-check the expected spread using the usual sqrt(p(1-p)/N) reasoning. Third gate: transpile specifically for the real backend I'm targeting, check the actual gate count and depth that results, and pull that backend's calibration report for whichever physical qubits the circuit landed on. Only then does it go into the hardware queue. I'd push back hard on any shortcut that skips straight from 'just wrote it' to 'submit to hardware,' because queue time is expensive and noisy, real hardware output can't tell you whether a bad result is your bug or the device's noise — you lose that diagnostic power the moment you skip the noise-free stages.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight from writing the circuit to submitting on real hardware
Not using the statevector simulator to isolate pure logic bugs first
Not checking the calibration report for the specific mapped qubits before submission
Treating simulator validation as optional rather than a required gate
keyPoints: Stage 1: statevector simulation isolates pure logic correctness
Stage 2: shots-based simulation validates realistic measurement statistics
Stage 3: transpile for the real target backend and check its calibration report
Skipping stages conflates logic bugs with hardware noise and wastes real queue time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a clear multi-stage pipeline with a logical order
Correctly assigns statevector simulation to catch pure logic bugs
Includes a transpilation + calibration-report check before hardware submission
Explains the cost of skipping stages (queue time, bug/noise confusion)

questions.title: Deciding when to invest in error mitigation vs. a different backend
questions.prompt: Your circuit's results on Backend A are noisy enough that you're considering adding readout error mitigation and zero-noise extrapolation. A teammate suggests instead just switching to Backend B, which has a better median error rate. How would you architect the decision between 'mitigate on A' and 'switch to B'?
questions.modelAnswer: This decision should be driven by what's actually causing the noise, not by which option sounds easier. Readout error mitigation specifically corrects systematic measurement-stage bias via corrected = M⁻¹·observed — it's the right tool if the dominant error source is misclassified measurement outcomes, and it's cheap to apply repeatedly once a calibration matrix exists. Zero-noise extrapolation targets gate-level error accumulated during the circuit itself, by deliberately amplifying noise via gate folding and extrapolating back toward zero — it's the right tool if the dominant error is from gate operations, not measurement, and it costs extra circuit executions at each noise-scale factor. Switching to Backend B only helps if B's actual calibration report (T1/T2, readout error, specific edge error rates for the qubits your circuit would map onto) is genuinely better for your circuit's specific connectivity needs — a better median error rate alone doesn't guarantee B has enough simultaneously good qubits/edges in the pattern your circuit needs. The architecturally sound approach: diagnose which error source dominates on A using the calibration report and a controlled test circuit, then decide — mitigation is often cheaper and faster to deploy than switching backends and requalifying a whole new device, but if A's connectivity or coherence for your specific circuit is fundamentally worse than B's, mitigation can't fix a structural hardware mismatch.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't let this become a coin flip between two options that sound equally plausible. I'd first figure out what's actually dominating the error on Backend A — is it mostly happening at the measurement stage, where readout mitigation is the right, relatively cheap fix, or is it gate-level error accumulating through the circuit, where zero-noise extrapolation is more appropriate but costs more circuit executions? I'd pull A's calibration report for the specific qubits and edges my circuit actually uses, not just the device's median numbers. Then I'd do the same for Backend B before assuming it's automatically better — a better median error rate doesn't tell you whether B has enough good qubits in the exact connectivity pattern my circuit needs. If A's problem is fixable with mitigation and B doesn't clearly solve a structural connectivity mismatch, I'd mitigate on A — it's usually faster to deploy than requalifying a whole new backend. But if A's qubits are just fundamentally worse for this specific circuit's needs, no amount of mitigation substitutes for better underlying hardware, and I'd make the case for B instead.
commonMistakes: Choosing between mitigation and backend-switching without first diagnosing the dominant error source
Trusting a device's median error rate without checking the specific qubits/edges the circuit actually uses
Assuming mitigation is always cheaper without weighing its added circuit-execution cost (ZNE)
Assuming a 'better' backend is automatically better for this specific circuit's connectivity needs
keyPoints: Readout mitigation targets measurement-stage bias; ZNE targets gate-level error
Diagnosis should use the real calibration report for the specific qubits/edges in use, not device medians
Switching backends only helps if the new backend is genuinely better for this circuit's specific needs
Mitigation is often cheaper/faster than requalifying a new backend, but can't fix structural hardware mismatches

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Distinguishes readout mitigation vs. ZNE by error source
Insists on diagnosing before choosing a fix
Notes median error rate alone is insufficient to judge Backend B
Weighs the cost/tradeoff of mitigation vs. switching backends

questions.title: Explaining shot-count tradeoffs to a non-technical stakeholder
questions.prompt: A product manager asks why your team can't just 'run it with way more shots so the results are perfect.' Walk through how you'd explain the real tradeoff behind shot count to someone without a quantum computing background, without being condescending.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer avoids both over-simplifying into 'it's complicated, trust me' and burying the PM in formulas. The core idea to convey: every run of the circuit is like a single poll of a population — asking more people (more shots) gets you a tighter estimate, but the improvement shrinks the more you already have. Going from 100 to a thousand runs helps a lot; going from a thousand to two thousand helps much less, because the precision only improves with the square root of how many runs you do, not one-for-one. And on real quantum hardware, each run isn't free — it costs real queue time and, for cloud access, real cost or allocated credits. So the honest framing is: we pick a shot count based on how precise the answer actually needs to be for the decision it's informing, not an arbitrarily large number, because past a certain point we're paying a lot more for barely any extra precision.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start from something they already understand — polling. If you want to know what percentage of people prefer A vs B, polling more people narrows your margin of error, but doubling your sample size doesn't halve your margin of error; you actually need about four times as many people to cut the margin in half. Running a quantum circuit more times (more 'shots') works the same way statistically. So 'way more shots' does help, but the returns shrink fast, and unlike a free online poll, every additional shot on real quantum hardware costs us real queue time and credits. I'd frame the actual decision we're making as: how precise does this specific number need to be for what we're using it for, and then pick a shot count that gets us there without paying for precision we don't need. If the PM pushes back, I'd offer to show the actual error-vs-shots numbers from our last run so it's a concrete tradeoff, not an abstract one.
commonMistakes: Dismissing the question as 'too technical to explain'
Overloading the PM with the exact sqrt(p(1-p)/N) formula instead of an intuitive analogy
Not connecting shot count to the real cost (queue time/credits) the PM actually cares about
Failing to frame the decision as 'how precise do we need this to be,' leaving it sounding arbitrary
keyPoints: Uses an accessible analogy (polling) rather than jargon or raw formulas
Explains diminishing returns: precision improves with sqrt(shots), not linearly
Connects shot count directly to real cost (queue time/credits)
Frames the real decision as matching precision to the application's actual need

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Uses an accessible, non-jargon explanation of diminishing returns
Correctly conveys the sqrt(N) scaling without requiring the PM to know the formula
Connects shot count to real cost/time tradeoffs
Avoids condescension while still being substantive

questions.title: Pushing back on a deadline that assumes zero hardware queue time
questions.prompt: A project lead sets a demo deadline assuming your circuit can be submitted and run on real IBM hardware same-day, with no allowance for queue time or job failures. How do you raise this concern constructively without just saying 'that's not possible'?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't just object — it replaces the unrealistic assumption with a concrete, defensible plan. First, acknowledge the goal (hitting the demo date) rather than treating the deadline itself as the problem. Then explain specifically what's unpredictable: shared real-hardware backends have genuine queue times that vary by provider load, and a submitted job can come back needing a fix (wrong transpilation target, qubit mapping issue, unexpectedly high error on the specific qubits used) that requires a resubmission, each with its own queue wait. Rather than leaving it abstract, propose a concrete mitigation: validate the circuit fully on the Aer simulator well before the deadline so hardware submission is the last step, not the first attempt; submit to hardware with real buffer time built in, ideally a day or more ahead of the demo; and have a rehearsed fallback (presenting the validated simulator result, or a previous hardware run) if the live hardware job doesn't come back in time. This reframes the conversation from 'this deadline is wrong' to 'here's how we hit the deadline reliably.'
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just flag the deadline as unrealistic and stop there — that reads as an obstacle, not a solution. I'd say something like: 'I want to make sure we actually hit this date, so let me walk through where the real risk is.' Then I'd explain that real quantum hardware is shared, so queue time isn't something we control, and that a submitted job sometimes needs a resubmit if something about the transpilation or qubit mapping didn't go as expected — each of those adds queue time we can't predict exactly. Then I'd pivot straight to a plan: we fully validate correctness on the simulator first, so the hardware run isn't where we're debugging logic; we submit to real hardware with a real time buffer, not same-day; and we have a fallback — showing the simulator-validated result or a prior successful hardware run — in case the live job doesn't land in time. That turns 'this is risky' into a specific plan the project lead can actually act on.
commonMistakes: Simply stating the deadline is unrealistic without offering an alternative plan
Not explaining concretely why hardware queue time is unpredictable
Failing to propose a fallback in case a live hardware run doesn't complete in time
Treating this as a confrontation rather than a planning conversation
keyPoints: Acknowledges the goal rather than just objecting to the deadline
Explains specifically why hardware queue time is unpredictable
Proposes simulator-first validation to de-risk the hardware step
Builds in time buffer and a concrete fallback plan

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Reframes the concern constructively rather than just objecting
Explains the real source of hardware-queue unpredictability
Proposes simulator-first validation and time buffer as concrete mitigations
Includes a fallback plan for the demo itself

questions.title: Disagreeing with a teammate's code-review comment on optimization_level
questions.prompt: During code review, a teammate insists you should always hardcode optimization_level=3 everywhere 'for safety,' even in the fast unit-test suite that runs against the Aer simulator dozens of times per CI run. You disagree. How do you handle this disagreement in review?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats this as a genuine technical disagreement to resolve with evidence, not a battle to win. Start by acknowledging the legitimate concern behind their suggestion — optimization_level=3 does produce the most reliable, smallest circuits, which matters for real hardware submissions. Then present the specific countervailing fact: level 3 is also the slowest to compile, and unit tests against the Aer simulator care about logical correctness, not final hardware gate count, so the extra compile time in a CI suite that runs dozens of times per run adds real, unnecessary friction with no corresponding benefit at that stage. Propose a concrete middle ground in the review comment: use a lower optimization_level (0 or 1) for the simulator-based unit tests, and reserve level 3 specifically for the transpilation step that happens right before real hardware submission, where its benefit is real. Offering to timestamp a quick before/after CI run with both settings turns the disagreement into a measured comparison rather than a stalemate.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd respond in the review thread by first agreeing with the part they're right about — level 3 absolutely matters when a circuit's actually headed to real hardware, since lower error there really does come from a tighter, shallower circuit. But I'd point out that our unit tests run against the exact Aer simulator, where we care whether the circuit's logic is correct, not whether it's been squeezed down to the smallest possible gate count — and level 3 is the slowest of the four settings to compile, which adds up over dozens of runs per CI pass for no real benefit at that stage. I'd suggest splitting it: keep a fast level (0 or 1) for the test suite, and apply level 3 specifically in the code path that transpiles for actual hardware submission. If they're still not convinced, I'd offer to run the CI suite both ways and show the time difference, so we're deciding based on a real number instead of just differing intuitions.
commonMistakes: Dismissing the teammate's concern outright instead of acknowledging where they're right
Not distinguishing between simulator-based testing and real-hardware submission needs
Letting the disagreement become personal rather than resolving it with a concrete proposal
Not offering to measure/verify (e.g., timing CI both ways) rather than arguing from intuition alone

Distinguishes simulator-based unit testing (cares about logic) from hardware submission (cares about gate count/depth)
Proposes a concrete split: low level for tests, level 3 for hardware submission
Offers to measure/verify rather than relying purely on argument

questions.title: Q# functors vs. Qiskit's .inverse()/.control()
questions.prompt: Explain what a 'functor' is in Q#, and why declaring an operation `is Adj + Ctl` is a fundamentally different guarantee than calling .inverse() or .control() on a Qiskit circuit object.
questions.modelAnswer: A functor in Q# takes an operation and produces a related operation without you writing new code for it. The two built into the language are Adjoint, which produces the inverse of an operation, and Controlled, which produces a version that only executes if a set of control qubits are all |1>. Declaring an operation `is Adj + Ctl` tells the compiler to generate both variants automatically — for a composed sequence of gates, the compiler reverses the sequence and substitutes each gate's own adjoint, which is exactly the mathematically correct way to invert a composed unitary sequence. The key difference from Qiskit's .inverse()/.control() is where the guarantee lives: those are library methods operating on already-built circuit objects at the Python level, and nothing in Qiskit's type system requires every gate or circuit to support them correctly by construction — it's something the library implements for gate types it knows about, and a custom gate's correct behavior under .inverse() is the developer's responsibility. In Q#, `is Adj + Ctl` is a compiler-checked declaration: if an operation's body contains something non-unitary and therefore non-invertible, like a measurement, the compiler rejects the `is Adj + Ctl` claim at compile time rather than letting the problem surface at runtime.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it as a library-level convenience versus a language-level guarantee. In Qiskit, .inverse() and .control() are genuinely useful methods, but they work on circuit objects you've already built, and it's on you to make sure a custom gate behaves correctly under them — Qiskit's type system doesn't enforce it. Q# takes a different approach: functors are built into the language itself. If I write `operation Foo(q: Qubit): Unit is Adj + Ctl`, I'm making a claim the compiler actually checks. For something simple like H, which is self-inverse, or a sequence like Ry then S, the compiler derives the correct inverse by reversing the sequence and adjointing each step — I never hand-write that reversal. And if I try to claim `is Adj` on an operation that calls a measurement internally, the compiler rejects it outright at compile time, because measurement isn't unitary and has no well-defined inverse. That compile-time rejection is the part that doesn't really have an equivalent in Qiskit — you'd only discover a bad custom .inverse() implementation at runtime, if at all.
commonMistakes: Treating Qiskit's .inverse()/.control() as equally rigorous as Q#'s compiler-checked functors
Not realizing the compiler itself rejects is Adj + Ctl claims on non-unitary operations
Assuming any operation can be marked is Adj + Ctl regardless of its body
Confusing functors (language-level operation transformers) with ordinary function calls
keyPoints: Adjoint produces an inverse; Controlled produces a control-gated version
is Adj + Ctl is compiler-checked and compiler-generated, not hand-written
The compiler reverses a gate sequence and adjoints each step for composed operations
Qiskit's .inverse()/.control() are library-level, not compiler-enforced

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines Adjoint and Controlled functors
Explains is Adj + Ctl as a compiler-checked declaration
Contrasts this with Qiskit's library-level .inverse()/.control()
Mentions non-unitary operations (e.g. measurement) being rejected at compile time

questions.title: What the Azure Quantum Resource Estimator actually outputs
questions.prompt: Explain what inputs the Azure Quantum Resource Estimator takes and what it outputs, and why its output is fundamentally different from what a simulator job returns.
questions.modelAnswer: You submit a compiled Q# program to the resource estimator target the same way you'd submit to a simulator, but instead of getting measurement results back, you configure qubit parameters describing the hardware you're asking it to assume: the physical qubit technology (e.g. gate-based superconducting-style assumptions vs. Majorana-based topological-qubit assumptions, each with different native error rates and gate speeds), the target logical error rate the whole computation needs to achieve, and the error-correction code parameters used to get there. Where a simulator job returns a histogram of measurement outcomes, a resource estimator job returns a structured report: the number of physical qubits required, total runtime, the number of logical qubits the algorithm needs, and the logical error budget breakdown across the computation. It fundamentally doesn't execute your program at all — it analyzes it and projects what running it would cost on a future, fault-tolerant quantum computer that doesn't exist yet, which is why 'what's the exact answer to this one input' and 'will this fit on a machine with N physical qubits' are different, and the estimator answers only the second.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd draw a clear line: a simulator tells you what your program computes; the resource estimator tells you what running it would cost on hardware that doesn't exist yet. You submit the same kind of compiled Q# program, but instead of waiting for a histogram of measurement results, you configure qubit parameters — what kind of physical qubit technology you're assuming, what logical error rate the whole computation needs to hit, and what error-correction code parameters get you there. What comes back is a report: how many physical qubits this would need, how long it would run, how many logical qubits the algorithm requires, and how the error budget breaks down. The big mental shift for people coming from simulator work is that this tool never actually runs your program — it's a projection, and the value of re-running it under different qubit-parameter assumptions is exactly the point: you get to ask 'how much would a better qubit or a different error-correction code actually save me' without that better qubit existing yet.
commonMistakes: Thinking the resource estimator executes the program and returns a computed answer
Not realizing qubit parameters are configurable assumptions, not fixed facts about real hardware
Confusing logical qubits (error-corrected) with physical qubits (the raw, noisy ones)
Treating a single resource-estimator run as 'the' definitive cost rather than one assumption set
keyPoints: Inputs: compiled Q# program plus configurable qubit parameters (technology, error rate, code parameters)
Outputs: physical qubit count, runtime, logical qubit count, error budget breakdown
It projects cost on future fault-tolerant hardware; it does not execute the program
Different from a simulator, which returns actual measurement results for existing/ideal hardware

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the inputs (qubit parameters)
Correctly describes the outputs (physical qubits, runtime, error budget)
Explains it does not execute the program
Contrasts this clearly with what a simulator returns

questions.title: Why teleportation doesn't send information faster than light
questions.prompt: A stakeholder read that quantum teleportation 'instantly' transfers a qubit's state and asks whether this could be used to send information faster than light. Using the actual 3-qubit protocol, explain precisely why it cannot.
questions.modelAnswer: The teleportation protocol entangles a Bell pair between sender and receiver, applies a Bell-basis change (CNOT then H) to the sender's message qubit and their half of the pair, measures both of the sender's qubits to get two classical bits m1 and m2, and then applies a classically-controlled correction (X if m2 is One, Z if m1 is One) to the receiver's qubit. A verified exact calculation shows each of the 4 possible (m1, m2) outcomes occurs with probability exactly 0.25, and critically, without those 2 classical bits, the receiver's qubit examined alone looks identical regardless of what the sender measured — it's in one of 4 equally likely post-measurement states, and you cannot tell which one without the classical information. The actual information transfer — telling the receiver which correction to apply — happens over m1 and m2, ordinary classical bits that can only travel at or below the speed of light, same as a phone call. Entanglement makes the correlation possible; it's the classical bits, not the entanglement, that make the correction (and therefore the useful outcome) possible, and classical bits can't exceed light speed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd correct the premise gently: nothing in this protocol moves information faster than light, and the protocol itself is the proof. The receiver's qubit, right after the sender's measurement and before the classical correction arrives, is in one of four equally likely states — and if you only look at that qubit by itself, with no access to the sender's two classical measurement bits, it's indistinguishable from any of the other three possibilities. There's no way to extract the teleported information from the receiver's qubit alone. What actually carries the information needed to recover the original state is the ordinary classical channel sending m1 and m2 — the same kind of bits you'd send over a phone line, bound by the same speed-of-light limit. Entanglement sets up a correlation in advance, but the correlation alone isn't a message; it's the classical bits, arriving no faster than light, that let the receiver apply the right correction and complete the transfer.
commonMistakes: Claiming entanglement itself transmits information instantaneously
Not identifying that the receiver's qubit alone is indistinguishable across all 4 outcomes without the classical bits
Forgetting the correction step depends on classical measurement results sent at or below light speed
Conflating 'the state is transferred' with 'information travels instantaneously'
keyPoints: The protocol requires 2 classical bits (m1, m2) sent via an ordinary classical channel
Each of the 4 measurement outcomes is equally likely (probability 0.25), verified exactly
The receiver's qubit alone, without the classical bits, is indistinguishable across all outcomes
Classical bits bound by light speed are what carry the actual usable information

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the 3-qubit protocol's structure
States the receiver's qubit alone is indistinguishable without classical bits
Correctly identifies the classical channel as the actual information carrier
Directly answers that this does not enable faster-than-light signaling

questions.title: Write a Q# operation with both Adjoint and Controlled
questions.prompt: Write a Q# operation `EncodeAngle` that applies Ry(theta) then S to a qubit and supports both the Adjoint and Controlled functors. Then write a second operation that calls it normally, calls its adjoint, and calls a controlled version with one control qubit. Explain what the compiler-generated adjoint actually does.
questions.modelAnswer: Declaring `EncodeAngle` with `is Adj + Ctl` tells the compiler to generate both functor variants automatically — I never hand-write the inverse or the controlled version. `Adjoint EncodeAngle(q, theta)` does not simply apply Ry(theta) and S in reverse order with no other change; the compiler reverses the sequence AND inverts each step, giving 'undo S, then undo Ry(theta)' — i.e. Adjoint S followed by Ry(-theta). That order reversal is exactly the mathematically correct way to invert a composed sequence of unitary operations, and it's exactly what I'd have to work out by hand if I were building this as a Qiskit circuit's .inverse() method myself. `Controlled EncodeAngle([ctrl], (q, theta))` takes an array of control qubits first, followed by the original operation's own arguments as a tuple, and only applies the whole Ry-then-S sequence if `ctrl` is |1>.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write EncodeAngle exactly like this, with the `is Adj + Ctl` clause right in the signature, because that's what unlocks both functors without me writing a second implementation. The part I'd specifically call out in an interview is what 'Adjoint EncodeAngle' actually produces: it's not 'the same two gates in reverse order' — it's 'the inverse of each gate, applied in reverse order.' So undoing 'Ry(theta) then S' means undoing S first, then undoing Ry(theta), which comes out to Adjoint S followed by Ry(-theta). That's the mathematically correct way to invert a product of unitaries, and the compiler derives it for me instead of me working it out and potentially getting the order wrong. For the controlled call, I'd note the signature shape: control qubits go in as an array first, and the original operation's arguments go in afterward as a tuple.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the is Adj + Ctl declaration, which is required to use either functor
Assuming the generated adjoint simply applies the same gates in the same order
Getting the argument-tuple shape wrong when calling the Controlled variant
Thinking you need to hand-write the inverse sequence yourself
keyPoints: is Adj + Ctl is required on the declaration to use either functor
Adjoint reverses the gate sequence AND inverts each individual gate
Controlled takes an array of control qubits plus the original arguments as a tuple
The compiler generates both variants; you never hand-write them

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly writes EncodeAngle with is Adj + Ctl
Correctly calls Adjoint and Controlled variants with correct syntax
Correctly explains the adjoint reverses order AND inverts each gate
Correctly describes the Controlled argument shape

questions.title: Write the 3-qubit teleportation operation in Q#
questions.prompt: Write the Q# `Teleport` operation that moves the state of qubit `msg` onto qubit `there`, using `here` as the sender's half of an already-entangled Bell pair. Explain what happens to `msg` after the operation runs, and why.
questions.modelAnswer: After `Teleport` runs, `there` holds exactly the state `msg` started in, but `msg` itself has been measured and destroyed in the process. This is required by the no-cloning theorem: quantum information cannot be copied, so teleportation necessarily consumes the original rather than duplicating it — if `msg` survived unmeasured with its state intact, you'd have two qubits holding the same unknown state, which is exactly what no-cloning forbids. The two `if` blocks implementing the correction are ordinary Q# control flow on classical `Result` values (`m1`, `m2`) — nothing quantum-mechanically special is happening there, the 'quantum' part of the protocol (entangle, then Bell-basis change) is already finished by the time those measurements and corrections run.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write it exactly in this order because the order matters: first entangle `here` and `there` into a Bell pair, then do the Bell-basis change (CNOT then H) between `msg` and `here`, then measure both of the sender's qubits to get m1 and m2, and only then apply the classically-controlled X/Z correction to `there`. On what happens to `msg`: it gets measured, and that measurement destroys its original quantum state — I'd explicitly connect this to the no-cloning theorem, because that's exactly why teleportation has to consume the original. If it didn't, you'd end up with the same unknown quantum state sitting in two places at once, which is provably impossible. I'd also point out the two `if` blocks are completely ordinary classical control flow on `Result` values — there's nothing exotic in that part of the code; all the quantum behavior already happened in the entangle-and-Bell-basis-change steps before the measurements.

Thinking msg survives with its original state intact after the operation
Not connecting the destruction of msg to the no-cloning theorem
Treating the classically-controlled X/Z corrections as something quantum-mechanically special rather than ordinary control flow

msg is measured and destroyed, consistent with no-cloning
there ends up holding exactly msg's original state after correction
The if-blocks are ordinary classical control flow on Result values

questions.title: Submitting a Q# program to three different Azure Quantum target types
questions.prompt: Write pseudocode/Q#-workflow showing how the same compiled program gets submitted to a simulator target, a resource-estimator target, and a real-hardware target in Azure Quantum, and explain what's identical and what's different about each submission.
questions.code:
# Same workspace.submit() call shape across all three; only the target string (and
# how you interpret the result) changes.
workspace.submit(program, target="simulator.target")
workspace.submit(program, target="microsoft.estimator")
workspace.submit(program, target="<hardware-provider>.qpu")
questions.modelAnswer: The submission code looks almost identical across all three categories — you select a different target string and the same workspace.submit() call routes the job appropriately. What differs is what each target actually does and what you get back. A simulator target computes the exact (or exact-up-to-approximation) result by tracking the state vector classically; it's free of real hardware noise and the right target for developing and debugging algorithm logic, since a wrong answer there is unambiguously a bug. The resource estimator target does not execute the program at all; it analyzes the compiled program and projects physical qubit count and runtime under configurable qubit-parameter assumptions, for hardware that doesn't exist yet. A real hardware (QPU) target routes to an actual third-party quantum processor through Azure Quantum's provider marketplace, giving a genuine quantum result subject to today's real noise, qubit counts, and queue times. A realistic project moves through these in order: simulator first for correctness, resource estimator once correctness is established to check feasibility, and real hardware only once there's a specific reason to see behavior under today's actual noise — running straight to hardware before validating on a simulator risks waiting in a real queue for a job that was going to fail anyway, and noisy hardware output makes a logic bug and a hardware error look identical.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out first that the code barely changes — it's the same workspace.submit() call with a different target string, which is deliberate: Microsoft designed it so your submission workflow doesn't change as the underlying hardware landscape changes. But I'd be careful to spell out what's actually different behind that similar-looking call. The simulator target gives you an exact computed result with no hardware noise — that's where I'd debug logic, because any wrong answer there is my bug, not noise. The resource estimator target is different in kind, not just degree: it doesn't run my program at all, it projects what running it would cost on future fault-tolerant hardware, under qubit-parameter assumptions I supply. The real hardware target is the only one that gives an actual physical quantum result, with today's real noise and queue times. I'd always sequence these in that order on a real project — simulator to validate logic, resource estimator to check long-term feasibility, real hardware only once there's a specific reason to see today's actual noise, because going straight to hardware risks burning real queue time on a job that a free simulator run would have caught as broken in seconds.

Submitting directly to real hardware before validating correctness on a simulator
Assuming the submission code differs significantly across target types (it mostly doesn't)
Not recognizing Azure Quantum's marketplace model means different QPU providers plug in as separate targets

Simulator target: exact computed result, no hardware noise, used for logic debugging
Resource estimator target: does not execute; projects future fault-tolerant hardware cost
Real hardware (QPU) target: actual physical result, subject to real noise and queue time

questions.title: A Q# operation fails to compile with is Adj
questions.prompt: A teammate's Q# operation refuses to compile when they add `is Adj` to its signature. The operation's body calls `M` on a qubit partway through. Diagnose why the compiler rejects this, and what they'd need to change to fix it.
questions.modelAnswer: The compiler is correctly rejecting this because `M` (measurement) is not a unitary operation, and `Adjoint` can only be generated for operations built entirely from unitary steps — there is no mathematically well-defined inverse of a measurement, since measurement collapses the quantum state and discards information irreversibly (you cannot un-collapse a state back to its pre-measurement superposition). Q#'s `is Adj + Ctl` is a compiler-checked claim, not a suggestion; if the operation's body contains anything that can't be adjointed, like a measurement, the compiler rejects the claim at compile time rather than letting the problem surface at runtime as Qiskit's library-level .inverse() might. The fix is architectural, not syntactic: the teammate needs to split the operation into a purely unitary part (which can be marked is Adj, and possibly is Adj + Ctl) and a separate part that performs the measurement, calling them in sequence from an outer, non-adjointable operation. There is no flag or workaround that makes a measurement itself invertible — the physics doesn't allow it, so neither does the type system.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain this as the compiler doing exactly what it's supposed to do, not a bug to work around. Adjoint means 'generate a valid inverse of this operation,' and a measurement has no valid inverse — physically, you can't un-collapse a quantum state back to what it was before you measured it, so there's no sequence of gates the compiler could generate that would undo an M call. Q# enforces that at compile time specifically so you find out now, rather than at runtime with some undefined or silently wrong behavior. The real fix is to restructure: pull the measurement out into its own operation, keep the fully unitary part of the logic in a separate operation that legitimately can be marked is Adj (or is Adj + Ctl), and call them in the right order from a wrapper that itself doesn't claim to be adjointable. There's no annotation or workaround that makes this compile as-is — the constraint is coming from the physics, and the compiler is just the messenger.

Not recognizing that measurement is fundamentally non-unitary and therefore non-invertible
Assuming this is a Q# tooling bug rather than a correct compile-time check
Trying to mark the whole operation is Adj without first separating out the measurement
keyPoints: Measurement (M) is non-unitary and has no well-defined inverse
is Adj + Ctl is a compile-time-checked claim, correctly rejected here
The fix is architectural: separate the unitary logic from the measurement into different operations
This is a physics-driven constraint, not a tooling limitation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies measurement's non-unitary nature as the root cause
Explains this is a correct compile-time rejection, not a bug
Proposes the correct architectural fix (separate operations)

questions.title: A team submits straight to real hardware and gets a wrong answer
questions.prompt: Your team submits a new Q# program directly to a real-hardware target and it comes back with a clearly wrong answer. Walk through why submitting to a simulator first, before touching real hardware at all, would have saved time either way — whether the bug turns out to be in the code or not.
questions.modelAnswer: If the bug turns out to be a genuine logic error in the Q# program, a simulator run would have caught it in seconds or minutes, with an exact, noise-free result making the error unambiguous — instead the team paid real hardware queue time to discover a bug that didn't need real hardware to find. If the code was actually correct and the wrong answer came from real hardware noise, the team still wasted the debugging effort of investigating the code for a bug that doesn't exist there, because without a simulator baseline to compare against, there's no way to immediately distinguish 'my code is wrong' from 'the hardware introduced error' — noisy real-hardware output makes a logic bug and a hardware error look identical at first glance. Either way, simulating first establishes a trusted baseline: a correct simulator result that then differs from the hardware result is genuine evidence pointing at hardware noise rather than a code bug, while a wrong simulator result points unambiguously at the code, in both cases saving the far more expensive step of diagnosing hardware behavior from scratch.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd make the case this way regardless of which way the bug turns out: if it's a real logic bug, the simulator would have shown it immediately, with an exact result, no queue wait, and none of the ambiguity hardware noise introduces — so we'd have fixed it in minutes instead of burning a real hardware queue slot to find it. And if the code was actually fine and the wrong answer came purely from hardware noise, we still wasted time, because without ever having run the simulator, we had no trusted baseline to compare against — we'd be stuck trying to figure out if this is a code problem or a hardware problem with no reference point. Running the simulator first gives us that reference point for free: if the simulator's correct and hardware disagrees, that's real evidence of hardware-side noise, not a reason to go re-read our own code for the tenth time. I'd propose this as a standing rule going forward, not just a one-off fix.
